Cilia and flagella. These are hair-like, motile projections that extend from the cell surface and generate movement by beating or rotating. Cilia are the shorter ones and appear in greater numbers, used for locomotion or to move fluids across the cell surface. Flagella are longer and typically present as a single structure, rotating like a propeller. Both structures contain a core of microtubules arranged in what's called a nine-plus-two pattern—that's nine outer doublets surrounding two central singlets—and they're anchored at the cell base by structures called basal bodies.

Basal bodies are actually modified centrioles. The outer doublet microtubules have protein projections called dynein arms that bind to adjacent doublets and generate movement. Between the doublets are elastic connectors called nexin links that constrain the sliding and help convert that sliding motion into bending waves. The coordinated activity of dyneins traveling along the cilium creates these bending waves that travel the length of the structure.

Most mammalian cells actually have a single, immotile cilium on their surface called the primary cilium. These aren't for movement—they function as sensory structures, acting like cellular antennae that detect chemical and mechanical signals. These signals are critical for development and homeostasis.

Prokaryotes have flagella too, but they're structurally entirely different—their flagella are protein filaments that rotate via a motor protein rather than sliding microtubules. Ciliary dysfunction causes a condition called primary ciliary dyskinesia, also known as Kartagener's syndrome, which results in chronic infections and infertility.
